summary:
Imagine being 225 million kilometers from home. A pain in your chest. An unusual reading. And twenty minutes of silence before anyone on Earth can respond. That is the real challenge of long-duration missions: radiation, isolation, altered gravity, and a hostile environment take their toll on the astronaut's body and mind.

ISIS was created to solve this problem. It is a smart wristband that monitors vital signs, blood oxygen saturation, temperature, sleep, stress, and cumulative radiation—both onboard the spacecraft and remotely. Its AI runs locally on the microcontroller, without relying on a connection to Earth, and analyzes sleep, activity, and stress along with self-reported mood to detect abnormalities and suggest specific actions. NASA doctors can also review the data from Earth.

Its impact is twofold: in orbit, it protects astronauts and prevents complications; on Earth, it generates knowledge so that NASA can develop better protocols, training programs, and spacecraft. ISIS doesn't just care for one person—it prepares humanity to live and work beyond Earth.
details:
NASA's crewed missions are becoming increasingly long-duration, and this brings new challenges: the behavior of the human body in the space environment, with effects from space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, and a closed, hostile habitat. These risks can lead to changes in the immune system, bone loss, cardiovascular events, and mental health issues.

The ISIS project is a smart wristband that uses sensors to monitor vital signs, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, body temperature, sleep duration, and space radiation, to monitor an astronaut's health both remotely and onboard the spacecraft. The wristband generates alerts via vibration and visual signals.

Its on-device AI, which runs locally on the microcontroller without relying on a connection to Earth, analyzes sleep patterns, activity levels, and physiological stress responses, and combines them with self-reported mood data to identify potential abnormalities. The AI suggests specific actions that the astronaut can take, which can also be monitored from Earth by NASA physicians.

The wristband consists of a microcontroller (MCU) that processes data from the sensors, an ECG sensor to measure heart activity, a PPG sensor to calculate heart rate and blood oxygen levels, an IMU to detect movement and physical activity, temperature and stress (EDA) sensors, a dosimeter to measure accumulated radiation, and a contact sensor that verifies the wristband is properly positioned. It also features memory for data storage, a low-power display, vibration alerts, secure Bluetooth communication, a battery with redundant protection, and a durable titanium casing designed for use in space environments.

ISIS pursues two objectives. In orbit, it protects the astronaut by monitoring their health, detecting abnormalities early, and suggesting specific actions to prevent complications. On Earth, it generates knowledge: the data collected allows NASA to understand how the human body responds to microgravity, radiation, and isolation. That knowledge translates into better protocols, better training, and better spacecraft. Ultimately, ISIS does more than just care for one person—it prepares humanity to live and work beyond Earth.

NOTE:

The name Isis refers to the Egyptian goddess of motherhood and healing. We do not intend to allude to any illegal group.
